title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
This page continues Euler's worked example of an elastic lamina (the classical elastica) loaded only by a terminal force. It sits inside his general force-balance method for flexible and elastic threads.

From the previous page:
- cos φ = 1 − x/a − n x²/a², where φ is the tangent amplitude measured from the point A where the axis is normal to the curve.
- B = (4n+1)A/a² and C = 2nA/a².
- dφ/ds = √(4n+1−4n cos φ)/a.

(1) Cartesian equation. Euler takes cos φ = dy/ds and sin φ = dx/ds, so dy = dx·cot φ. Write c = 1 − x/a − n x²/a². Then 1 − c² = (x/a + n x²/a²)(2 − x/a − n x²/a²). Multiplying by a⁴ gives 2a³x + (2n−1)a²x² − 2n a x³ − n²x⁴. Hence dy = (a² − ax − nx²)dx / √(2a³x + (2n−1)a²x² − 2nax³ − n²x⁴). This is the elastica as an elliptic-type quadrature, with a quartic under the root.

(2) §XXXIII, radius of curvature. The radius is r = ds/dφ = a/√(4n+1−4n cos φ). Solving the quadratic for x gives x = (a/2n)(√(4n+1−4n cos φ) − 1) = a²/(2nr) − a/(2n). Equivalently, the curvature 1/r = (a + 2nx)/a² is a linear function of the abscissa. Euler stresses this as the 'eximia proprietas' common to all elasticae: curvature is proportional to the distance from the line of action of the force, i.e. bending moment ∝ curvature.

(3) Classification. Euler rewrites the radicand as 4n+1−4n cos φ = 1 + 8n sin²(φ/2) and splits by m = |8n|:
- 8n = m > 0: the root is always real, so φ can grow without bound.
- 8n = 0: the elastica is a circle, r = a.
- 8n = −m with m < 1 (continued on the next page): φ is again unbounded.
- m = 1: the limiting (separatrix) case.
- m > 1: sin²(φ/2) < 1/m, so the amplitude is bounded and the curve is the inflectional type.

This reproduces the species of elastic curves from the 1744 Methodus inveniendi (Additamentum I).
errors: No error on this page; the algebra for dy/dx, r, x(r) and the half-angle identity all check.

Not an error, but a redundancy: the case 8n>0 is not genuinely distinct from −1<8n<0. Shifting φ→φ+π turns 1+8n sin²(φ/2) into (1+8n)(1 − (8n/(1+8n)) sin²(φ/2)), which is the m<1 case with a rescaled a. Euler treats them as separate cases without remarking this.
On the next page the transcription reads r = a cos½Φ for m=1. The formula gives r = a/cos(½Φ), i.e. 1/r = cos(½Φ)/a. This is either a misprint in the original or a transcription slip.

ideas.what: Cartesian differential equation of the elastica as a quadrature with a quartic radicand
Curvature is linear in the abscissa: x = a²/(2nr) − a/(2n)
ideas.modern_name: Bernoulli–Euler law (bending moment proportional to curvature) for the elastica

ideas.what: Classification of elasticae by the sign and size of the modulus 8n in √(1+8n sin²(φ/2))
ideas.modern_name: Inflectional vs non-inflectional elastica, separated by a separatrix (pendulum analogy)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler 1744; the pendulum analogy to Kirchhoff 1859
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum I (species of elastic curves)

deep.surprise_reason: The page re-derives, inside the new force-balance framework, the 1744 elastica results and classification. These are well documented, e.g. by Truesdell in Opera omnia II.11. Nothing on the page is new.
transcription_corrections: 'sin.½φ²' in the original means sin²(½φ), not sin(½φ²).
In the x-formula, 'cos φ' should read 'cos. φ' for consistency; this is trivial.
The 'r = a cos ½Φ' on the next page should be checked against the image; mathematically it should be r = a/cos ½Φ.
